deep.reconstruction:
This page is not a computational sheet. It is a page of Gauss's scientific diary (the 'Tagebuch'), entries no. 92–100 in Klein's numbering. They run from July 1798 (Göttingen) to November 1799 (Braunschweig). Each entry is a terse Latin announcement of a result, and the page itself contains no derivations. The entries are:

(92) Göttingen, July 1798. 'On the lemniscate we have obtained most elegant things exceeding all expectations, and by methods that open an entirely new field.' The context is the lemniscatic sine and its inverse, with ϖ = 2∫_0^1 dx/√(1−x^4) = 2.62205755… The previous page contains Fourier expansions of sin lemn and arc-sin-lemn. This entry concerns the analytic theory of the lemniscatic functions: addition and multiplication, division of the lemniscate, and periodicity in two directions.

(93) Göttingen, July 1798. 'Solution of the ballistic problem': projectile motion with air resistance.

(94) Göttingen, July 1798. 'I have made the theory of comets more perfect': orbit determination.

(95) 'A new field in analysis has opened to us, namely the investigation of functions etc.' The date is smudged or struck, probably Oct. 1798.

(96) Braunschweig, 14 Feb 1799. 'We have begun to consider higher forms': forms of degree greater than 2.

(97) Braunschweig, 8 Apr 1799. 'We have derived new exact formulas for parallax.'

(98) Braunschweig, 30 May 1799. 'We have verified to the eleventh figure that the arithmetic-geometric mean between 1 and √2 equals π/ϖ. Once this is demonstrated, an entirely new field in analysis will certainly be opened.'
In modern terms, set a_0 = √2, b_0 = 1, a_{n+1} = (a_n+b_n)/2, b_{n+1} = √(a_n b_n). The common limit is M(√2,1) = 1.198140234735592…, and π/ϖ = 1.198140234735592… The numerical identity is therefore correct well beyond 11 digits.
The identity is equivalent to Gauss's later theorem 1/M(a,b) = (2/π)∫_0^{π/2} dθ/√(a²cos²θ + b²sin²θ). With a = √2, b = 1 this integral becomes ∫_0^1 dx/√(1−x^4) = ϖ/2 (my filling, not on the page).
The previous page already shows '1,198' and series computations leading to it.

(99) Braunschweig, Sept 1799. 'We made excellent progress in the principles of geometry': the foundations of geometry and the parallel postulate, i.e. non-Euclidean geometry.

(100) Braunschweig, Nov 1799. 'We discovered many new things about arithmetic-geometric means.'
errors: No mathematical errors. The claimed equality M(1,√2) = π/ϖ is true; it is the AGM–elliptic integral identity, which Gauss proved in December 1799 (next page: 'Medium Arithmetico-Geometricum ipsum est quantitas integralis', Dec. 23).
The phrase 'usque ad figuram undecimam comprobavimus' is a numerical verification only. The proof is explicitly deferred ('qua re demonstrata').

results.what: Lemniscatic functions: elegant results and new methods (July 1798)
results.modern_name: Lemniscatic elliptic functions, double periodicity, complex multiplication/division of the lemniscate
AGM–complete elliptic integral relation (Gauss's AGM theorem), lemniscate constant
AGM theory, theta functions, modular aspects

deep.surprise_reason: This is a page of Gauss's famous mathematical diary, published by Klein in 1903 and discussed extensively since (Gray's translation, among others). Entry 98 on M(1,√2) = π/ϖ is one of the most celebrated and well-known Gauss items.

checkable.asserts: The lemniscate constant ϖ = 2∫_0^1 dx/√(1−x^4) = Γ(1/4)^2/(2√(2π)) ≈ 2.6220575543 (difference ≈ 0).
1/M(√2,1) = (2/π)∫_0^{π/2} dθ/√(2cos²θ+sin²θ) = ϖ/π, the integral form of Gauss's AGM theorem.

transcription_corrections: 'qua re demonstrata' – the manuscript reads 'quare demonstrata' (one word); the sense is the same.
The year '1799' is written small at the right margin after 'Br. Febr. 14'.
The bracketed '[-Oct-][?]' after 'functionum etc.' is a smudged/blotted date, most likely 'Oct.' (1798).
The symbol transcribed as ϖ in 'π/ϖ' is Gauss's ω-like 'varpi' (the lemniscate half-period), not an ordinary ω.
The marginal fragments on the left ('ut nihil', 'Gott. Jun.', 'attractione', '1,198', etc.) belong to the facing previous page.
